1567468,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.1.1.1,1949-10-03,unmatched,,,,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,THANKSGIVING DAY ADJOURNMENT,,"I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. Monday next, October 10, will be Thanksgiving day. In common with many others, I feel sure that the Prime Minister has a good deal to be thankful for, and I was wondering whether he would permit the members of this house to have next Monday as a holiday.
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime

Minister): The Prime Minister is always susceptible to any suggestion that comes from the other side of the house. I take it that the applause means that there are several in the house who agree with the suggestion which has been made. If it appears to be the desire of the house, the government will take the necessary steps to see to it that when the house adjourns on Friday night it stand adjourned until three o'clock the following Tuesday.

,,,Mr.  W. Chester S. McLure@Queens,

column2: There are 125 in the Rocky Mountain House band of the Sunchild Cree Indians (treaty Indians) who live on a reserve thirty miles from Rocky Mountain House. There is also a group of 200 Chippewa Indians (nontreaty) who wander in the foothills. So far as is possible in the light of their highly nomadic life, the same facilities are extended to both groups by the directorate of Indian health services.

column1: (Mr. Martin.]

The medical care of these people has been provided by a doctor of Rocky Mountain House on a fee-for-service basis. The doctor has seen patients in his office and has attended them in Rocky Mountain hospital. It has not been convenient to him to attend on the reserve.
A local dentist has provided dental services on a fee-for-service basis,

2 and 3. The doctor's accounts for professional services have been paid in accordance with the prevailing schedule of fees which is applied uniformly across Canada where professional attention is provided on a fee-for-service basis. However the doctor has not been satisfied with the schedule of fees. In June 1948 the directorate of Indian health services offered to pay him a per annum stipend if this would be more agreeable to the doctor but he did not reply to this offer. Recently he signified his intention to cease services to Indians except as private patients.
The rate paid to the Rocky Mountain hospital is $5 per day for adults and $1.25 for newborn children. This rate was established May 1, 1948, and has not been under discussion since that time.

column2: There is every reason to believe that arrangements for hospitalization at Rocky Mountain House are satisfactory. The Indian health service regional superintendent in Alberta is continuing to negotiate with local physicians for the provision of professional services.

,Social Credit,,Ernest George Hansell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b7be8f86-27c2-4da9-a780-2d2bb5edfa31&Language=E&Section=ALL
1567497,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.8.2,1949-10-03,647c88fa-1673-4147-88b3-b42105bc54e3,ca.m.2918,Mr. Claxton:,Minister of National Defence,PUBLIC STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS OF DIPLOMATIC SERVICE,,,The general rule is that the government accepts responsibility for speeches on matters of public policy made by officers of the external affairs service, at home and abroad. This general rule is subject to exception according to the circumstances in which speeches are made. So, for example, when an external affairs officer, in speaking, indicates that he is doing so in his personal capacity, or where he speaks as chairman of an international conference, committee, or other body, he is clearly not representing a government view, as such. Moreover the government may disclaim statements made by external affairs officers inconsistent with government policy.

1567551,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.22.2,1949-10-03,9ea559ad-4beb-4e15-9d33-3bf98265f437,ca.m.1689,Mr. Belzile:,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance,RENT CONTROL,,,In so far as the wartime prices and trade board is concerned:

At the inception of dominion-wide rental control all real properties, with the exception of lands and premises used solely for farm purposes, were made subject to the regulations. From time to time the regulations were relaxed by exempting from either all or part of the regulations a certain class of real property or a certain class of lease of real property. So hotel accommodation was exempted on April 7, 1947; summer cottages, winter chalets, etc., on February 23, 1948; commercial accommodation on March 8, 1948; buildings completed by new construction after January 1, 1947, on June 19, 1947; and self-contained housing accommodation let to a person who was not the tenant on November 1, 1948, on that date. The various exemptions applied to the property itself or the lease thereof as was appropriate in each case. Since these exemptions all were effected by general amendment of the regulations, and the landlords in order to take advantage of the regulations do not have to communicate with the wartime prices and trade board, and since there never has been and is not yet any complete tabulation of every rental in effect in Canada, it is impossible to determine
Questions
the number of residential properties which have been affected by these various exemptions.

The wartime prices and trade board, by its order effective on April 14, 1947, permitted landlords who suffered grievous hardship from their inability to recover possession of their own housing accommodation to apply to a commissioner for an exemption permitting them so to recover possession in accordance with the laws of the province in which the accommodation is situated. It is the duty of the commissioner to consider the hardship of the landlord and also that of the tenant, if he were evicted, and either to grant or refuse such application. To the 31st of August, 1949, commissioners have granted such applications in the following numbers:
British Columbia
Alberta
Saskatchewan
Manitoba
Ontario
Quebec
New Brunswick
Nova Scotia
Prince Edward Island

It should be emphasized that such exemptions are not decontrol but merely the granting of permission to the landlord to recover possession for his personal occupancy. So long as the tenant remains in occupancy the maximum rental ceiling is still in effect, and thereafter the premises are not rented but owner-occupied.

Effective November 1, 1948, the wartime prices and trade board permitted landlords who needed housing accommodation for their own personal residence and who had owned it since November 1, 1947, to give to the tenant six months' notice to vacate on forms provided by the board. A copy of such notice must be filed in an office of the board prior to service. To August 31, 1948, such notices have been filed in the following number:
British Columbia
Alberta
Saskatchewan
Manitoba
Ontario
Quebec
New Brunswick
Nova Scotia
Prince Edward Island
Again it is pointed out that such notices to vacate are not indicative of residential properties which have been decontrolled. They simply represent demands for possession filed

in the board's office. If they were served on the tenant, and in all probability the large majority were so served, the maximum rental ceiling applied to the residential accommodation until the tenant vacated, and thereafter the accommodation was owner-occupied. In fact in both these cases and those described in the preceding paragraph the board by a special and individual order on each filing prohibits the landlord from renting or selling the accommodation for a lengthy period.

column2: Has the government or the Department of Transport received any advice to the effect that the Canadian National Railways intends to discontinue the movement of its transcontinental trains to and from Kamloops Junction to Kamloops station?
If so, what reasons are given for this decision?
Will the government or the Minister of Transport intervene to have the railway continue the service to and from Kamloops as formerly?

column1:
,Progressive Conservative,,Mr. Fulton:,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=bd7064c6-90b2-4e0a-9a8f-1c4d781bb30e&Language=E&Section=ALL
1567562,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.25.1.1.2,1949-10-03,e2b15c2f-35a6-4e4e-8e52-a4357fdebc0d,ca.m.9148,,Minister of Transport,CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS,KAMLOOPS,JUNCTION TO KAMLOOPS STATION,1.
column2: Yes, by passenger traffic department, special circular No. E-16/49. This circular was sent to the board of transport commissioners and to the Department of Transport.

The Canadian National Railways advise that until the fall change of time train No. 3, one of Canadian National's two westbound transcontinental trains, operated via Kamloops. Withdrawal at the conclusion of the summer service of one of the two steamers plying between Vancouver and Victoria necessitated the schedule of No. 3 being shortened one hour in order to permit this train to make steamer connections. It was not possible to shorten the schedule of No. 3 sufficiently without eliminating the Kamloops Junction to Kamloops station movement.

It is not the policy of the government or the Minister of Transport to intervene in matters which relate to the internal operation of the Canadian National Railways, but it is open to any individual or organization to make representations to the board of transport commissioners with respect to changes which may be made from time to time in railway services.

1567600,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.31.1.1.2,1949-10-03,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,LABOUR CONDITIONS,CANADIAN PACIFIC EMPLOYEES,STRIKES OF,That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the immediate establishment of a royal commission to examine into the whole question of the pension rights of Canadian Pacific employees who were involved in the strikes of 1918 and 1919, the said commission to have power to determine the settlement that should be made of the matters in dispute and to whom and in what manner any pension adjustments should be made, as recommended by Mr. H. S. Johnstone, Industrial Relations Officer of the federal Department of Labour, in his report to the Minister of Labour under date of December 7, 1945.

He said: I am satisfied that this is a motion the purpose of which has the support of hon. members in all parties in this house. In fact I believe it has the support of the majority of hon. members, and I hope they will vote accordingly. Its purpose is to try to find a way to rectify a gross injustice perpetrated thirty years ago. It may seem strange that an injustice outstanding so long should still be the subject of debate in this House of Commons, but hon. members who were here prior to the last election, and those who were here prior to the election of 1945, will be familiar with the story of the employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company whose pension rights were denied to them because of their participation in certain strikes of 1918 and in the Winnipeg general strike of 1919.

I realize that hon. members who have been here as long as I have, or longer, may feel that the story is well known to them and need not be rehearsed; but so as to refresh their memories, and so as to bring the grievous nature of this injustice to the attention of the ninety or one hundred new members, I should like to touch upon some of the highlights.

As some hon. members know, there were in the years 1918 and 1919 a number of sporadic strikes, particularly in western Canada from Fort William through to the Pacific coast. In addition to these strikes, many of which were of short duration-one that I know of in Kenora, Ontario, lasted for only eighteen hours-there was the general strike in Winnipeg in May and June of 1919. Railway employees became involved in these strikes, particularly in the general strike of 1919. Those involved were mainly the shop crafts, the trainmen, express employees, and a few others. I am not going into the story of the strike itself, nor shall I argue its merits one way or another at this late date; but the fact is that when employees of various companies and corporations returned to work, questions arose about their pension rights. In due course employees of other large corporations and bodies in the city of Winnipeg had their pension rights restored. I refer particularly to the employees of the Canadian National Railways, a few provincial government employees, quite a number of telephone employees, and also employees of the city of Winnipeg, including policemen and firemen. All those employees were on plans which at that time were noncontributory. Yet in a very short time the pension rights of the employees of all these other employers to whom I have referred were reinstated. But not so the employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. They were informed that a rule in the pension plan, which had been in effect since 1903, brought about a condition under which a break in service would cut off any prior pension rights. Another rule stipulated that no one starting to work over the age of forty years could become eligible for pension.

The joint effect of these two rules was that Canadian Pacific employees who were over forty years of age in 1919 lost all the pension rights they had earned up to that time, and were denied entry into or the enjoyment of any pension benefits they might otherwise have earned after 1919. I emphasize that there is that group of men who thirty years ago were forty years of age and over who lost their pension rights in their entirety. In addition to that, employees who in 1919 were under forty years of age, while in due course permitted to enter the pension plan which
Labour Conditions
was brought into effect in 1937, and while given certain rights from 1919 to 1937, were denied all rights they had earned prior to 1919.

This means that we now have quite a number of older men in the first category about which I have spoken who are retired employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, some of whom had thirty, forty or fifty years of service-I know of one who had fifty-four years-but no pension whatsoever. In addition we have men retiring now, year by year, and going on pension, but that pension is reduced from what it should be. They receive only such rights as they have earned since 1919. They lose the rights they earned prior to that year.

For reasons which have been detailed here so often, and which are well known particularly to hon. members from railway centres from Fort William to the Pacific coast, the men affected have felt this was a grievous wrong, and one which should be rectified. They made their own efforts over the years, particularly in 1936, 1937 and 1938, when negotiations were under way in connection with the new contributory plan which was put into effect on January 1, 1937.

During the negotiations for that plan the general chairmen, who represented the trade unions to which these men belonged, tried to have the company reinstate the men who had lost their rights because of the so-called break in service in 1919. The company refused. Even after the new pension plan was agreed to, and even after it came into effect on January 1, 1937, the same general chairmen who had negotiated for the men in respect of the new contributory plan continued to negotiate, and appealed on behalf of the men who were affected because of the 1919 situation.

I emphasize that point because it is sometimes alleged that the unions, and the leaders representing the men, accepted this as an accomplished fact when they agreed to the new pension plan. This is not so.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Stanley Howard Knowles,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Humphrey Mitchell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97&Language=E&Section=ALL
1567602,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.31.1.1.4,1949-10-03,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Knowles:,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,LABOUR CONDITIONS,CANADIAN PACIFIC EMPLOYEES,STRIKES OF,I have on my desk, and was about to deal with, a copy of a letter sent out on October 18, 1939, over the signature of Thomas Broad, addressed to all the officers and members of the affiliated lodges-and in this connection the affiliated lodges are those of the C.P.R. system federation, No. 125- telling the members of the affiliated lodges what they had been trying to do on their behalf, and expressing regret that thus far Mr. Coleman, on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and the others
Labour Conditions
for whom he spoke, had not seen fit to meet their request.

In the letter sent out by Mr. Broad, in which he quoted from a report placed in his hands by Mr. A. McGovern and Mr. J. A. Bell, who were respectively chairman and secretary of the subcommittee dealing with the question of the reinstatement of pension rights, this statement is made by the general chairmen, who carried on representations on behalf of the men:

We have kept in close touch with this matter for a very considerable period of time, always encouraged by the hope that sufficient improvement might take place in the financial condition of the company to enable us to realize the firm conviction which we have always held, that, in such improved conditions at least, some relief might be forthcoming.

One of the main arguments used by Mr. Coleman was that to meet the request made would cost $1,250,000 and, their revenues being what they were in the mid-thirties, the request could not be granted. May I point out at this moment that my efforts in connection with this whole problem have divided themselves into two parts: On the one hand I have tried to persuade the government to find some way to rectify the injustice perpetrated in 1919, and on the other hand I have tried to get legislation to prevent the recurrence of this kind of injustice.

With respect to the second matter of trying to get legislation to prevent this from happening again, hon. members who were here in the last parliament will know that that has been achieved. It is now the law of the land that-

I am reading from subsection 2 (b) of section 4 of the labour code. That amendment was agreed to by this house on June 17, 1948. Hon. members will remember how often I asked for that protection. I want to impress upon hon. members who have heard me speak time and time again on this subject the fact that there is a difference between the bill I brought in year after year, the principle of which is now on the statute books, and the fact that the men who were deprived of their rights in 1919 still have not had that injustice rectified.

It is the opinion of the undersigned that the employees have established strong claims for consideration. Speaker, I am going to say only a few words in this debate, because I do not think the case made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) requires support, I do not believe his case could be improved by anything that either I or any member could say in support of it.

I rise merely to draw attention to a question which has been asked in connection with the appointment of a royal commission. This question was asked by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll), and ] believe the same question has been put in more positive form by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Macdonald). The hon, member for Inverness-Richmond has asked whether the findings of a royal commission, if enforceable, could be legally binding upon the company. Then, if I heard him correctly, the hon. member for Edmonton East gave il as a categorical statement that the findings of a royal commission could not be legal.

Surely when a royal commission is appointed we do not ask whether its decisions or its findings-it does not make decisions; it makes findings-can or cannot be enforced. That is not the purpose of appointing a royal commission. About a year age the government appointed a royal commission on prices. Was it a prerequisite to the appointment of that royal commission tha1 its findings could be enforced in a court of law? It could make findings against certain companies.
We have appointed hundreds of royal commissions. As a matter of fact, a royal commission is appointed to ascertain facts, following which the government may or maj
not act upon such facts thus ascertained by the royal commission. That is the whole point of this proposed appointment.

Let me go back to the appointment of Mr. Johnstone, who was appointed to investigate this matter and make recommendations. Evidently his recommendations were not binding. Nevertheless he was appointed and he made a finding to the effect that the case should be further investigated by a royal commission, such body or individual having greater moral authority than he would have.

I am positive that, if the investigator had said he did not think a royal commission should be appointed, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) would bring that forward at once as a reason for not appointing such royal commission. He would base his case solely upon that finding. However, the investigator did not do that; on the contrary, he submitted to the Department of Labour that this was a case of importance sufficient to warrant the appointment of a royal commission to ascertain further facts. I suggest that the Department of Labour, or the government on the advice of the Department of Labour, could not go far astray in accepting that advice.

Hon. members will understand that I have some knowledge of the 1919 strike, and had knowledge of it before some hon. members who now sit in the House of Commons resided in Canada. This problem strikes at the very roots of contractual obligations as we understand them. I have a vivid recollection as a boy, in Hamilton, of the 1919 strike. I could name the actors in that great labour drama. I think the mistake in Winnipeg was that they took the wrong advice. When you make a contract, it is a contract; when you break it, there is no longer a contract. You have to renegotiate just as they had to do in 1926 after the general strike in Great Britain.

I am sincere when I say that if by following the advice of my hon. friend we could give, not justice but a measure of support to these men, I would certainly go along with him. Do not accuse me of supporting big industry or monopoly capitalism, whatever that might mean, and all that sort of thing, when I say that this is not our money, but that it belongs to somebody else. As was stated by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll), if a royal commission or some other person should make a recommendation, this House of Commons has no power to carry it out. As I have said before, it is far better to tell people the blunt truth as you understand it even though it may not be very popular.

I believe quite sincerely that the setting up of a royal commission would be nothing else but window-dressing. It could not do anything for the people concerned. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) said something about the right to strike-I do not know where he read that; so did the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston). That is not the point. The point is that there was a breach of contract. This money belongs to somebody else because it was a noncontributory system. While the powers of parliament are great, there is a limit to those powers.

Noseworthy (York South):,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,CANADIAN PACIFIC EMPLOYEES,STRIKES OF,From 1942 to 1945, Mr. Speaker, I had the pleasure of listening to various debates on this question. I am amazed to find a minister of labour taking the position that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has taken this afternoon, particularly a minister who over the 45781-30
Labour Conditions

years has prided himself on carrying his trade union card and being so closely identified with trade unions, and also in view of the efforts that trade unionists belonging to the railway trades have themselves made.

There are one or two statements made by the minister to which I want to call attention. First of all he charges that those who are pressing this matter today are simply kidding these poor men who suffered an injustice thirty years ago. I submit that, by the same process of reasoning, if the minister is right, then he was also kidding these men when he appointed an officer of his department for the purpose of finding out whether a royal commission was necessary to investigate the matter. I do not see how the minister can escape that conclusion. Of course that officer was appointed just prior to an election, but that is no excuse. I submit that the minister cannot escape the conclusion that, if those who are waging this fight today are kidding these people, the minister also was kidding them, and he must have known he was kidding them.

The minister laid great stress on the fact that this is somebody else's money. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) merely tried to show that the money actually belonged to the employees by reason of their years of service, and was to some extent compensation over those years for that service. There is another point I wish to make. If people are going to talk about C.P.R. money being somebody else's money, I want to place on the record what this parliament and other parliaments have given to the C.P.R. in the past. I quote from the Canada Year Book, 1942, which brings the figures up to December 31, 1940. In terms of acres of land, up until December 31, 1940, according to pages 587 and 588 of the Canada Year Book, the dominion government granted the C.P.R. 26,109,043 acres of land. The provinces of Canada gave to the C.P.R. 10,847,333 acres, or a total of 36,956,376 acres. Incidentally, that is nearly 30 million acres more than was given over the years to what is now the government-owned railway, the Canadian National system.

In addition to that, the government gave cash subsidies to the C.P.R. up to December 31, 1940, of $99,860,984. The provinces gave $14,587,592. Various municipalities gave $4,610,157, making a grand total of $119,058,733, or about $31 million more in cash subsidies than was given to the publicly-owned system. Considering the amount of money that has been given to the C.P.R., it is difficult to understand how the minister can defend his position and defend the C.P.R.
The minister made one other statement, which apparently is a new argument, that contracts had been broken in the old strike,

and that the trade union movement had taken the correct measures to try to rectify the situation. In reply I say that the trade union movement and those former employees of the C.P.R. are entitled to some help from parliament. 1567689,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.31.1.1.91,1949-10-03,84760b33-550e-42e1-a3f1-3d89c8ec15c8,ca.m.7602,Mr. Paul E. Cote (Verdun-La Salle):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour,LABOUR CONDITIONS,CANADIAN PACIFIC EMPLOYEES,STRIKES OF,I do

not intend to be very long, Mr. Speaker. I should like particularly to answer a few of the points that have been raised by hon. members of the party of the mover of the resolution. Before I do so I think it would be appropriate to review briefly events of some importance which have taken place ever since this subject has been under consideration, either directly or indirectly, by the federal Department of Labour.

The resolution has been inspired by reason of the difficulties which arose out of the Winnipeg strike of 1918 and 1919 in which employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway were involved. A general strike started about the beginning of May, 1919, and lasted for about a month and a half. After it was ended most of the C.P.R. employees were rehired by the company as new employees, and that is the crux of the question.

As a matter of record I may say that not more than a month after the end of the strike the Manitoba government saw fit to set up a royal commission, which of course was within the jurisdiction and responsibility of that government. That royal commission commenced sitting in July, 1919, and held its last sitting on September 10 of that year, after having heard a number of witnesses and conducted independent inquiries into several activities related to the strike. The final report was made to the lieutenant governor in council on November 6, 1919.

The question raised in the resolution now under consideration was allowed to pass, without action being taken on the grievances of those C.P.R. employees in regard to the loss of pension rights, until after January 1, 1937. At that time a new pension plan for C.P.R. employees came into operation, based upon contributions by both labour and management. It was after the new plan had been considered by a joint council of representatives of the company and the employees that the brotherhoods realized the implications of this new plan as against those employees who had taken part in the 1919 strike and who had been rehired after reaching the age of forty.

This matter was dealt with in consultations between the brotherhoods and the C.P.R. for close to two years after the new pension scheme came into force on January 1, 1937. That was the right way to handle this matter,

as the minister mentioned in his short address. This is a matter for negotiation between labour and management. In any case, this negotiation procedure went on for practically two years, from 1937 to 1939, but did not bring about the concrete results for which the C.P.R. employees were looking. In 1944, twenty-five years after the end of the strike, during which period of time nothing had been done through the usual channels of collective bargaining except during 1937 and 1938, the matter was brought to the attention of the house. I give credit to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for having raised the question here. I should like all hon. members and the country to realize that the government has been most sympathetic to the case of those my hon. friend had in mind when he raised this question in 1944; and I shall attempt to show that in the course of events which followed the Department of Labour and the minister did their utmost within the bounds of their jurisdiction to impress upon the company that certain wrongs should be redressed.

1567693,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.31.1.1.95,1949-10-03,84760b33-550e-42e1-a3f1-3d89c8ec15c8,ca.m.7602,Mr. Cote (Verdun-La Salle):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour,LABOUR CONDITIONS,CANADIAN PACIFIC EMPLOYEES,STRIKES OF,If my hon. friend will allow me to proceed I shall be glad to give my views on what would be the advantage or otherwise of setting up a royal commission.

It was in 1944, I said, that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre brought up the matter while the house was discussing the labour angle of the war appropriation bill. At that time the basic argument he presented was that since other important bodies

such as our own government, the provincial government, the city of Winnipeg and the Canadian National Railways had solved a similar problem to the advantage of the employees concerned, there was no reason why the C.P.R. should not fall into line and abide by this precedent, if I may call it that, which had been set by the others concerned. What was the answer of the minister? Let me quote what he had to say on that occasion. As a matter of fact he did not undertake to do anything more than he and his department have been doing since 1944. Here is what he said, as it appears at page 2508 of Hansard for May 1, 1944:
I shall be very glad to do whatever lies within the power of my department to bring to the attention of the railway concerned the observations made by my hon. friends this afternoon.

Other hon. members had given their views on the matter, including the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Fort William. This reply by the minister clearly indicated that the ground on which the minister might act was the humanitarian ground. Nothing was said in one way or another which would permit the inference to be drawn that the minister committed himself to set up a royal commission, or that he committed himself to force the hand of the Canadian Pacific Railway if any favourable conclusion was reached which might be used in that way.
After that what happened? On May 19,

column2: negotiations were initiated with the company. My hon. friend has seen the file, which I may say is one of the thickest in the industrial relations branch of the department. On that date a communication was addressed to Mr. W. M. Neal, vice-president of the C.P.R.; and thereafter the minister took it upon himself to suggest to the company that a meeting should be arranged to be attended by representatives of the brotherhood of railway and steamship clerks, the brotherhood of express employees, the brotherhood of railway trainmen and another organization known as the Canadian merchant service guild, which had made representations. It was suggested that these people should meet with the responsible railway officials under the auspices of the Minister of Labour, and try to thresh out this whole matter and find some satisfactory basis of agreement.

The hon. member for York South has said that throughout the transactions, since 1944, and more particularly when he decided to send a special investigator in the person of Mr. Johnstone to Winnipeg, the minister was kidding. As I have tried to show during my observations, the Johnstone report has provided a new ground from which to start fresh negotiations with the company. This inquiry has provided a new picture of the situation, and has allowed the department to re-establish its contact with the company and thus to begin negotiations anew. There can be no doubt that this was done in the best of good faith, and for the best of purposes.

I believe I have set out a fair outline of what the stand has been by the Department of Labour throughout the past five years, since this matter has been brought to the fore. The department has been trying to act in the capacity of negotiator between the company and the employees; at the same time it has never admitted any direct responsibility, other than that of its deep interest in and sympathy with the fate and the distress of a certain number of men.

In 1904 when the pension fund was set up by the company-and this is the focal point of the whole situation, from a legal standpoint-it was done of its own free will, and without any interference from any governmental group or union representatives. This was done through the wish of the company to better the welfare of its employees- at least it was so taken at the time. The company remained entirely responsible for it.
tMr. Cote (Verdun-La Salle.)

It seems to me the employees might have been well advised to decide before 1937 to show a direct interest in the management of the fund. I do not know whether they did or not, but the fact is that they did not have any link whatsoever with the administration of the fund until 1937, when the new plan was set up. The company was free to set up the scheme and to manage it as it chose, under its own rules and formulae. This is the situation which confronted the employees at the time of the 1919 strike.

After thirty years there is nothing the Department of Labour can do beyond its own jurisdictional bounds. The department has done its utmost, and I suggest this once more illustrates its deep interest in matters of concern to labour. Since 1944 we have accumulated a file which challenges in physical content any other file in our department. At least we have done that. The department claims that the only corrective measure which can be obtained would be through the procedure of negotiations. We have exhausted all those procedures.

Now we are faced with the suggestion set out in the resolution that a royal commission be set up. It is true that the recommendation of the Johnstone report is to that effect, and the hon. member has quoted the concluding paragraph in the report which, it seems to me, indicates clearly that the industrial relations officer, Mr. Johnstone, thought there was sufficient information of importance and concern which he had gathered to justify a more complete inquiry. It was his suggestion that a royal commission be set up, and he was speaking of course as an industrial relations officer.

It is the responsibility of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and the government to decide whether a royal commission should be resorted to to settle a problem such as this, which is not within the competence and jurisdiction of this government or parliament. The responsibility of government obliges it to take an attitude one way or another; and the attitude that has been taken is that the setting up of a royal commission would serve no useful purpose whatsoever.

Now that all possible grounds of negotiation with the company have been covered, what would be the use of permitting this inquiry to prolong itself over months, perhaps years? What would be the purpose of spending public money to an unknown extent?- because, in the past, some royal commissions have been quite costly. What would be the purpose in doing all this unless there was some way of carrying out the findings of such a commission to relieve a situation which affects these employees who lost their pension rights with the Canadian Pacific in 1919?

That is the position taken by the government. The Department of Labour wishes labour to know that it has done everything humanly possible to co-operate in this matter and to attempt to arrive at a satisfactory solution. The department cannot go any further without interfering with the jurisdiction of somebody else. If we set up a royal commission and tried to implement its recommendations there is no doubt that in one way or another-my hon. friends know what I am referring to-the matter would come before the courts and it is as clear as crystal that it would be declared ultra vires. We have no right to go beyond what we have done already in an attempt to bring about a satisfactory conclusion.

I conclude by reminding my hon. friend that his interest in this matter since 1944 has brought some results. He has achieved one of his purposes by having placed on the statute books labour legislation which would prevent any such action being taken in the future as a result of a strike or lock-out. He is now asking us to interfere with something that happened thirty years ago, to adopt a procedure which would force the company to take retroactive action back that far. He is asking us to attempt to remedy a situation which is essentially a matter of collective bargaining.

The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) mentioned this afternoon that he could not go so far as to set up a royal commission because jurisdiction does not lie with the federal government. Therefore, I think the hon. member would be wise not to go further with this matter. His resolution has served his purpose in bringing about a useful discussion and has given the government an opportunity to voice its views on the matter. The hon. member should not insist on this matter going any further. It has become insoluble because action could not be forced on the company.

1567724,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.31.1.1.126,1949-10-03,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre):,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,LABOUR CONDITIONS,CANADIAN PACIFIC EMPLOYEES,STRIKES OF,I will be very brief in closing the debate on what I regard as an extremely important matter. I noted that it was still put forth as an argument a good many times, especially by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), that the money involved is someone else's money. As I tried to indicate by means of an interruption in the minister's speech, I agree that it is someone else's money. In fact I agree with Mr. Johnstone that morally the money belongs to the men.

May I point out that right now the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is having the experience of paying out money that is in the same category. Reference has been made repeatedly to the new contributory pension plan that came into effect on January 1, 1937. A man who retired from the C.P.R. in 1948, and is today on pension, is receiving a pension made up in part of what he has earned out of the contributory fund since January 1, 1937, and in part of his stake in the noncontributory funds prior to January 1, 1937. We are simply asking that the recognition that there is money there in the general funds of the C.P.R. that belonged to certain men be extended to cover these other men.

Another argument put forward forcibly by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cote) was to quote considerably rule 13, from the old rules, and contend that there was a voluntary staying away from work on the part of these men. Of course whether or not it was voluntary is one of the matters in dispute. That is one of the reasons a royal commission is needed. In his report Mr. Johnstone says that was one of the matters that had to be considered by the Canadian National Railways, and they decided

that, in view of all the circumstances surrounding the Winnipeg general strike, they could not make a blanket decision that all these men stayed away on a voluntary basis. Mr. Johnstone says that some of these men, for example, reported for work during the day and found that the place had been closed because of difficulties and disturbances earlier in the morning. The position that the hon. member for Verdun-La Salle (Mr. Cote) took is challenged by the report of Mr. Johnstone, which again is a reason why the whole question should be gone into more thoroughly, more objectively, and more judicially, as we feel it can be done by a royal commission.

I listened with interest to the recital which the parliamentary assistant gave of the things the Department of Labour has done, but it seemed to me that at times he was putting a very good front on it. As I recall the months between December, 1945, and May, 1946, that is the time between the date of the Johnstone report and the reply of the C.P.R., all that is shown in the correspondence that has been tabled in the house is that the Minister of Labour shipped the Johnstone report to the C.P.R., and then there were several letters asking the C.P.R. to send their reply because it was being demanded in the house. Finally, in May, the report came back, and the C.P.R. reply with it.

Despite the recital that the hon. member has given this afternoon, I am not satisfied that the government has done what he says, namely, its utmost. He can say that the government has done all the things he has indicated, but until the government is prepared to set up a royal commission to go into these matters the government cannot say that it has done its utmost. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the name of justice for these citizens of Canada who have suffered this injustice so long, I plead with the house to call upon the government to give the consideration asked for in the resolution. Now that the debate on the matter is over I hope that the house will approve the resolution.

KNOWLES    REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. MITCHELL IN DEBATE,,"Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. During the debate this afternoon the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and I had an exchange which ended amicably when he accepted my word as to certain statements that I had made. However, I rose during that exchange and indicated that I was prepared to accept his challenge to bring Hansard down before the day was over, and show that what I had quoted him as saying was on the record. The matter had to do with my saying that in 1944 the Minister of Labour was not satisfied with representations that I brought on the floor of this house from local railway lodges, but that if he received a request from the Canadian heads of the unions involved his department would act on such a request. The minister at first denied making the statement. Later he implied that this had been said to me in confidence. Still later he accepted my word. I now wish to document my statement by pointing out that this all appears in Hansard of July 24, 1944. The list of local lodges to which I referred takes about a column of page 5267. Then on page 5269 the minister said:
The hon. gentleman read a certain number of' letters from local organizations.
Then he went on in his usual way to refer to them and ended up by saying:

But if I were to get a request from the parent organization-and as my hon. friend from Cape Breton South knows probably as well as I do, they always deal with their national organization in matters of this kind-I should be glad to endeavour to arrange a conference if possible between the company and the organizations concerned.

A similar statement was made by the minister a few moments later, as recorded on page 5271 of the same day. I will not take the time of the house to read his repetition of his insistence on any request coming from a parent organization, but I thought it only fair that it should be clear that the statement I attributed to the minister was not something said in confidence but a statement made on the floor of the house.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Stanley Howard Knowles,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78&Language=E&Section=ALL

1567732,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.33.1,1949-10-03,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. Angus Maclnnis (Vancouver East) moved:,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,That, in the opinion of this house, the government should seek the co-operation of the provinces for the purpose of formulating a program of social security that will be national in scope, adequate in its provisions, and that will cover all citizens of Canada in every circumstance where the individual or the family is, for any reason, deprived of the opportunity of earning a living.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am extremely glad to have the opportunity of moving this resolution and of expressing my views in regard to the subject matter of it. I think this is the fourth session of parliament in which I have had this, or a similar, resolution on the order paper, but because of the urgency of government business at other sessions, which eliminated private members' days, or because my resolution was too far down on the order paper to be reached, this is the first opportunity I have had of moving it in the house.

Perhaps it is well that the resolution should be moved now. We have had an election in which every party represented in this house has had a social security plank in its program, and as far as I have been able to learn through following the reports of speeches of the candidates of the various parties they too advocated a policy of social security improvement. As far as I can remember, most of the members from my own province told their constituents that if they were sent to represent the constituencies in this house they would advocate social security improvement on the floor of the House of Commons.

I have tried, Mr. Speaker, to make the resolution as short and as explicit as words could possibly make it. I do not wish to have any misunderstanding of what I am urging. Briefly the resolution asks this house to endorse a nation-wide social security program.

For convenience in debate the resolution may be divided into four parts. First, it asks the government to seek the co-operation of the provinces for the purpose of formulating a program of social security. In my opinion this is the obvious first step since social service or social security is by our constitution a provincial responsibility. However, it has been demonstrated that it is a responsibility which most of the provinces are not able to discharge.

Second, the resolution proposes that our social security program be nation-wide in scope. That is, as far as the federal government is concerned, the benefits paid and the conditions under which they are paid shall be the same in every province in Canada.

Third, that our social security program be adequate in its provision; that is, that the benefits, in the absence of any other income, shall be such as to assure a minimum but adequate standard of living.
Fourth and last, that the social security benefits should be available to every citizen of Canada who is deprived, by reasons beyond his control, of the opportunity of earning a living.

The points I have outlined are the essential requirements of a social security program. Indeed, I think they are all the essential requirements of a social security program for Canada and I believe that anything less would not be adequate. I could produce many reasons, economic and social, as to why social security measures provided by the state are becoming increasingly essential to larger and larger sections of our people. I do not believe it is necessary for me to take the time to do that. Almost everyone realizes that they arise out of economic and social development, economic and social progress, if you like, over which we have little control. But apart from these reasons there are humanitarian considerations which provide sufficient grounds for this parliament enacting such a program. As far as this house is concerned I should like to believe that the humanitarian considerations would be sufficient in themselves.

May I draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that an additional reason why we are entitled to look to the state for assistance is that when the state feels it is in need it can and does require not only the service of its citizens but their lives as well. I claim therefore that if the state can call upon a citizen in its time of need, the citizen should be able to call upon the state in his hour of need. While I refer to ""the state"", I do not want the house to conclude that I refer only to the federal government. It will be noted that in the resolution I ask that the federal government seek the co-operation of provincial governments for the purpose of working out a complete system of social security.

I do not propose either that everything should be centralized here in Ottawa. However, in co-operation between the dominion and the provinces, it should be made clear as to what the provinces are prepared to do and what the dominion government is prepared to do in order that among the eleven governments we would have a complete system of social security.

When the federal government of 1945 laid the green book proposals before the provincial governments, an attempt was made along the lines I am now suggesting. Failure at that time does not mean that we should
accept failure for all time to come. The proposals made in 1945 by the federal government are as valid today as they were then.

Not only that, but I am convinced that the need for social security is more pervasive among our people today than it was at that time. May I quote briefly from the proposals of the government of Canada, which are generally referred to as the green book proposals. The opening section of the government's proposals, entitled ""National Problems and Objectives"", outlines what the government in 1945 saw as the national problems, and the means it intended to take to solve those problems.
At page 7 of this book are found these words:
The government has clear and definite views on how these objectives can be obtained.
The objectives were, in the main, prosperity and security for the people of Canada. It continues:
These views may be summarized very briefly as, first, to facilitate private enterprise to produce and provide employment;
Secondly, to promote-
And I would ask hon. members to notice this one carefully
-to promote bold action by the state in those fields in which the public interest calls for public enterprise in national development;
Thirdly, to provide through public investment, productive employment for our human and physical resources when international and other conditions adversely affect employment; and.
Fourthly, to provide on the basis of small regular payments against large and uncertain individual risks, for such hazards and disabilities as unemployment, sickness and old age.
I am dealing tonight only with the fourth item. I should like to read further from page 8, two short paragraphs which really state my position as well as or better than I could state it myself:

Because Canada is a federal state these responsibilities are shared by the federal and provincial governments. This division of responsibility should not be permitted to prevent any government, or governments, in co-operation from taking effective action.

What I am asking tonight is not only that the house approve my resolution, but that it approve what was put forward by the government of 1945, and that this government take effective action as quickly as possible. May I read on:
To devise a working co-operative arrangement to a common end, in harmony with our federal system, is the main purpose of this conference.
That is the conference which was called to discuss these proposals. It continues:

It is with these considerations in mind, and in search of common ground for agreement, that the government presents its proposals. These proposals assume a broad federal responsibility, in co-operation with provincial governments, for establishing
Social Security

the general conditions and framework for high employment and income policies, and for support of national minimum standards of social services. They also assume that provincial governments should be in a financial position to discharge their responsibilities adequately.

My resolution is quite in harmony with the proposals and, I must presume, with the policies of the government of that time. Because of the size and constitution of this country, decentralization of administration to the provincial level is in my opinion not only desirable but imperative. People intimate with local conditions can make a much better job of dealing with human beings than can those who are remote. It makes a great deal of difference to the person concerned whether he is treated merely as a case with a number or whether he is treated as a human being.

I have been a trade union official or a public representative for almost the whole of the past thirty years. As such it has been my opportunity to come in contact with the boards administering the social security legislation in my own province, such as the old age pensions board and the workmen's compensation board. I am bound to say I have always found that these officials consider, with both sympathy and imagination, the problems coming before them. If they have not done a better job it is, I am satisfied, ninety-nine per cent because the law they have had to administer has not made that possible. I would not be dealing with this question realistically if I did not point out that considerable social security is provided at the present time by the dominion and the provinces. Under federal and provincial jurisdiction we have old age and blind pensions. Wholly under federal control we have unemployment insurance and family allowances-

1567734,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.33.3,1949-10-03,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. Maclnnis:,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,That comes under the provinces. And there is certain assistance in the way of health grants. Under the provinces we have workmen's compensation, mothers' allowances, welfare legislation of various kinds and health and hospital services. However, these social security measures whether under provincial or dominion jurisdiction have developed in a haphazard way. Many of these measures have been put into operation, not so much because of the government's belief in them as because it was thought politically expedient to provide them. I submit that the time has come when we should find out what is required and see what we can do in an orderly and planned way.
There are tremendous gaps in our social security program. For example, there is no provision for sickness or invalidity. A worker who is out of a job because there is no work
Social Security

is entitled to unemployment insurance, but if the same worker is out of a job because he is sick, he is not entitled to anything. Indeed if he is taken sick while drawing unemployment insurance benefits the benefits stop. Surely a person who is unemployed because of sickness is more in need of assistance than one who is just unemployed. A man in such circumstances has the additional expenses associated with illness.

Our old age pensions provide for people who have reached the age of 70 years provided they are practically destitute. But surely the person who has not reached the age of 70 years is just as much entitled to assistance if because of illness or infirmity he is unable to provide for himself? Surely these are gaps which a country such as Canada should be ready to concede ought not to be tolerated?

As a beginning of an adequate social security program I think we should lay it down that need should be the criterion for state assistance and not a particular category or class into which a person might fall. Following that, the assistance given should be such as to provide a minimum standard of health and decency. I do not know of any better words to use, and those are the words generally used by welfare organizations. We should strive to set a minimum standard below which no family income should fall.

May I point out that no country can escape the social consequences of poverty. If we do not provide an adequate family income, whether we like it or not we shall have to make provision for more police, more jails, more courts, more reformatories, more hospitals and more of all those institutions the need for which is created in large measure by poverty and the consequential family breakdown. The general opinion among people experienced in social service administration or those engaged in social welfare work is that the greatest cause of family breakdown is poverty. If we do not eliminate poverty in one way we shall have to take care of it in another. Perhaps I should quote an authority on this point. In 1943, Dr. L. C. Marsh was engaged by the government to prepare a report on social service for Canada. I have that report in my hand and I quote from page 119 as follows:

Finally, the obvious but vital point must be made that social security payments are not money lost. The social insurances, and even some straightforward disbursements like children's allowances, are investments in morale and health, in greater family stability, and from both material and psychological viewpoints, in human productive efficiency. They demand personal and community responsibilities; but in the eyes of most of the people who are beneficiaries, give a more evident meaning to the
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
ideas of common effort and national solidarity. It has yet to be proved that any democracy which underwrites the social minimum for its citizens is any the weaker or less wealthy for doing so.

I think we can all agree with that. 1 urge this house to show by its approval of this resolution that it believes that the time has arrived for the elimination of the effects of poverty, if we cannot, at this time, get down to eliminating its causes, by expanding and co-ordinating the social services of this country so that all those people who need assistance will be covered. It is possible that a social security program such as I have suggested will require amendments to our constitution. If so, those amendments should be sought without delay. But, even while we are preparing any amendments that we think necessary, we should see what we can do in co-operation with the provinces, because I am convinced that a great deal can be done without amendment of the constitution. As far as I can remember, from reading the proposals made in 1945, there was no mention of amendments being necessary for what the dominion government proposed at that time.

Other countries less wealthy than Canada are ahead of us in this regard. Perhaps I need only mention the United Kingdom and New Zealand. In the United Kingdom, despite their difficulties, all parties are agreed that their social security program is necessary and must be maintained. Following the United Kingdom election of 1945 the Labour government put a social security program into effect. The Conservative party in its election program, ""The Right Road for Britain"", has laid it down that the country's social security program will be not only maintained but expanded if that party assumes office after the next election. I merely point out that today people everywhere are convinced of the necessity of providing social security.

There are some people in Canada who oppose any further extension of our social services, but I do not think we should pay much attention to them because they have opposed every extension of social security in the past, and they will do so in the future. Perhaps the most comprehensive report that has ever been made on social security is what is known as the Beveridge report, prepared by Sir William Beveridge in 1942. He laid down three guiding principles for social security. The first principle reads as follows:

. . . that any proposals for the future, while they should use to the full the experience gathered in the past, should not be restricted by consideration of sectional interests established in the obtaining of that experience. Now, when the war is abolishing landmarks of every kind, is the opportunity for using experience in a clear field. A revolutionary moment in the world's history is a time for revolutions, not for patching.

I suggest to the government that world revolution is not yet complete. It is proceeding in every country, and perhaps faster than anywhere else in the western nations where people have the opportunity of thinking, and thinking aloud. I suggest to the government that what they need now is not to put patches on our present social security but to take bold steps to build a comprehensive program such as I have suggested. The second principle laid down by Sir William Beveridge is:

. . . that organization of social insurance should be treated as one part only of a comprehensive policy of social progress. Social insurance fully developed may provide income security; it is an attack upon want. But want is one only of five giants on the road of reconstruction and in some ways the easiest to attack. The others are disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness.
I think that if we make a frontal attack on want we will go a long way towards conquering these other giants that Sir William Beveridge mentions. The third principle reads as follows:

. . . that social security must be achieved by cooperation between the state and the individual. The state should offer security for service and contribution. The state in organizing security should not stifle incentive, opportunity, responsibility-

I have never seen the case for the abolition of the means test put better than that. I have never been able to see the logic of insisting that a person should not be allowed to help himself. I do not want to mention specific cases tonight, but at the moment I have a case, which I am taking up with the war veterans' allowance board, where a veteran has had his allowance cut off because his wife went to work during the war at the age of sixty-five, and the income she produced, which was used for shingling their home, as they told me, was not reported to the war veterans' allowance board. Personally I do not see who could be hurt by allowing these people to add something more to their income. If they made something more than what is allowed under the income tax structure they could be taxed in the same way as other individuals.

Up to this point I have not said anything about how a social security program should be financed. I am dealing with broad principles and not with details. I do not believe that I have any illusions about how measures of this kind are paid for. They are paid for out of the national income. That in turn comes out of national production, and the national production is the product of those who work. When we provide social services of any kind we are providing material things such as food, clothing, shelter and services of one kind or another, which must be produced by those who are working.
Social Security

Perhaps I could express my own ideas of how such things can be paid for by a simple illustration. It is easier to think in small numbers than in large ones because when a thing gets very large it sometimes becomes complex, and it is difficult for the ordinary person to understand it.

Let us suppose that the population of the country was composed of the three members behind me and myself. It would be a dull world, but this is just a supposition. Suppose it was composed of those four people and we were all working. We would all be producing our own keep, the others anyway, and I suppose they would see that I did. Let us suppose that they decided to pension me off because I had reached an age where my youthfulness was a thing of the past. There would be no place under the sun where my keep could come from except out of their labour.

The same is true in our national affairs; you merely have to multiply that by ten million, or whatever figure you like. The result is the same. The money is merely the measure of the goods and services provided by the rest of the community. For instance, if you keep your mother-in-law you pay for her upkeep yourself; but if she receives an old age pension the community keeps her. That is the difference; you are throwing some of your burden on the community. I say that, because there is an idea abroad that there is some mysterious source from which food, shelter and clothing can be paid for without taking it from those who produce it or have claims of ownership to it. There is no such way.

1567743,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.33.12,1949-10-03,6dec82d6-fab3-438b-b40f-c7720a93d8c1,ca.m.5451,Mr. Howard C. Green (Vancouver-Quadra):,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members appreciated the way the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) placed his resolution before us for consideration this evening. I should like to say a few words in support of the main theme of the resolution, which in my understanding is that now is the time for steps to be taken to formulate a program of social security which will be national in its scope. That is the part of the resolution that particularly appeals to me.

I think it very timely that we should consider this topic now, in this first session of the twenty-first parliament, for several reasons. The first reason is the attitude of the Canadian people toward questions of this sort. I believe Canadians generally, and certainly Canadians on the Pacific slope, desire an all-embracing program of social security. They hope the different governments throughout the country will take steps to see that such an all-embracing program is put on the statute books at the earliest possible moment. Then, too, I think the attitude of the Canadian people is that they are willing to pay for such a program. Provided that the payment is spread evenly and fairly across the country, I believe Canadians are willing to pay for such a plan.

I also believe their attitude is one of intense dislike of the means test. There is something very un-Canadian about it. Many elderly people come in to ask me about making application for old age pension. These people who have worked hard for a lifetime, who have brought up families at great sacrifice, and who while they have very little money have great natural dignity and pride, in reality are the type of people who have built this nation. Yet when they are faced with the necessity of disclosing their resources, they hesitate to do so. They are hurt by the thought that they must tell

someone what assets they have, and must show that their children are not able to support them. The whole idea of a means test is repugnant to such people, and I repeat that they are the very finest citizens we have in this country.

That attitude should be well known to the government. Hon. members will even find it at page 37 of the proposals of the government of Canada at the dominion-provincial conference of 1945, in what is commonly called the green book. There we find this statement:

The means test is generally recognized as undesirable after a certain age. It has been noted that about forty per cent of all persons of seventy years of age and over make application, satisfy the means test requirements and receive pensions. There is little doubt that a very considerable number in addition are not able entirely to support themselves, but are dependent upon their family, and refrain from applying for pensions because of the embarrassment occasioned by the means test.

I repeat, I believe the Canadian people are anxious to get rid of this means test. They would prefer to permit our senior citizens to improve their position by working, if able to do so. Not only would that be a help to the elderly people themselves; it would also be a help to the country at large, and I believe it is still generally the feeling of our people that thrift should be encouraged. So my first reason for saying that this resolution is timely is the attitude of the Canadian people.

My second reason is the attitude of the Canadian political parties. I believe every party in Canada is deeply interested in welfare measures. I do not wish to be political tonight, but if I had one criticism of the C.C.F. more than another it would be that at times they speak as though they believe they are the only Canadians in public life who are interested in the welfare of the people. That is not so. The members of all parties are vitally interested in welfare measures. If they are not interested in people they do not get elected, or if they get in once they do not stay elected. We are all deeply concerned with welfare measures. There may be some difference of opinion as to how those measures can be best enacted and put into effect, but I do not believe the hearts of the members of any one party in Canada are a bit bigger than the hearts of the members of other parties. My second reason, therefore, for my stand is the attitude of the Canadian political parties. Every party in this house is pledged up to the hilt to bring in a national social security program. I have here the advertisements of the government party, and also those of our own. The other parties are pledged in the same way.
Now that we are here, let us get busy and do something about carrying out those pledges.

My third reason for saying that this resolution is timely is that there is now a great move on in the United States in the direction of social security plans. I have here the last issue of U.S. News and World Report. In it I find a most interesting article entitled ""Bigger and Better Pensions?"" which contains this statement:
In congress, plans are being pushed to make 1950 ""social security year.""

Our neighbours to the south are taking great interest in this type of plan, just as we are in Canada. In the United States within the last few days we have seen the settlement of the Ford strike on the basis that there will be pensions for the employees of the company. That really is my fourth reason for my stand this evening. I believe that pensions are coming in industry. In some cases the companies may pay the whole pension, as I believe is being done by the Ford company. In other cases they may make a partial contribution. But there is no doubt that this whole question of pensions in industry is one of the important ones to be faced by the public men on this continent at this time.

Even if pensions in industry come into effect, many Canadians will not be covered by such a plan; considerably over half could never possibly be covered by any such plan. Therefore consideration must be given by governments to ways of bringing in a plan that will cover all of the Canadian people. Furthermore, I think difficulty may arise in determining the fields to be covered by government and by industry; there is no clear-cut demarcation of what group will be covered by industry and what group will be covered by government measures. We must try to figure out what division there should be.
The article to which I referred a few moments ago ends with this paragraph:
Decision, in favour of one system or two systems, is what is forming now.
That is, a decision between pensions in industry and government pensions.

If liberal, but costly, private pensions paid for by industry are given to millions of workers, then, in the opinion of many officials, there will be little chance of getting employers to help pay for a more liberal government system for all. Result may be high pensions for some workers, relief lines for others.
I read that paragraph to show that this whole question is worthy of a great deal of investigation and thought. Those are four reasons advanced for the consideration of hon. members.
Social Security

In my own opinion we should have in Canada a contributory pension system under which men and women would contribute as they work, employers would contribute, and the various governments would contribute. Then Canadians would be entitled to draw as of right benefits in adequate amounts when they were needed. I believe that such a plan would make it possible for us to provide pensions at sixty-five years of age, without a means test, or earlier if people are unable to work further; to provide sickness and disability benefits and health insurance; and to give extended unemployment insurance benefits. There would also have to be similar benefits for those Canadians who are unable to make contributions.

That is my idea at the moment of the way in which this problem could best be solved by Canada. I believe that is the Canadian way in which to work out a solution. But certainly at this session some steps should be taken by the government. There is no doubt at all that they should raise the ceiling on old age pensions to conform with the raise in the pension itself which was put through last spring. I do not believe there is a member in this house who would not be in favour of raising that ceiling. That is one statute that should be passed at this particular session. In addition to that, I believe consideration should be given to the broader plans for meeting this problem. I hope that the government, through the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), will agree to the terms of this resolution. Then if the minister will go ahead and take whatever steps are necessary to bring about the required legislation, I think he will find general support from all sides in this chamber.
