1567744,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.33.13,1949-10-03,15f7b640-a209-4f80-8dd3-69851bfeb8ad,ca.m.5033,Mr. Lionel Bertrand (Terrebonne):,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) on the subject of social security and I am pleased to have this opportunity of taking part in the debate.

It would be, I believe, extremely important for the government to request the co-operation of the provinces in order to work out a nation-wide social security plan. It would probably take some time to apply such a plan, so that it would be better, I think, to go about it by stages, so as to gradually, year by year, bring about a permanent solution of some aspect of the social problem.
I am in favour of a social security plan as elaborate as possible, for it is my considered opinion that communism can never enter homes in which peace, joy and happiness are to be found.
Social Security
I would however like to point out that I have myself placed on the order paper, under No. 7, a resolution which particularly concerns destitute invalids and cripples.

I first submitted this resolution in 1946; it was discussed and met with the approval of the house but was never adopted. Since then, the resolution has appeared in the order paper at every session but due to certain circumstances or to special legislation, it was never considered. I am confident, however, that this resolution, which I consider very important, will be considered and given the general approval of this house during the present session.

A class of people who are particularly neglected are the infirm and the invalid. If their families are too poor to give them appropriate care or if, because of their infirmities, they are unable to earn their own livelihood, these infirm and invalid become forsaken and outcast. Municipalities are unable to do anything to help them. The provincial statutes do not provide for them. I have found nothing in the federal statutes which might authorize the central power to help them.

Cripples and invalids are excluded from the labour market. They are turned away for reasons having to do with security, output and production. Deprived of employment, or occasionally doing some odd job, can an invalid ensure his own subsistence? If he has a wife and children, his plight becomes tragic and his distress is increased by the humiliation of having to beg and live on public charity.

Cripples and invalids deserve their share of well-being. I suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) that he should consider the matter and have a survey made of the number of cripples and invalids without means of support, with a view to recommending an adequate and proper allowance, to be paid jointly by the central government and the provinces. If it so happened that the provinces declined to accept such a nation-wide plan, I believe the dominion government should assume the cost itself.

In a country as wealthy as ours, where life has become quite comfortable, there is no reason for leaving the underprivileged class in destitution and discouragement. Besides, our national security program will never be complete unless it includes special consideration for cripples and invalids.
In connection with social security, I have a suggestion to make to the Minister of
National Health and Welfare. I believe that the term ""old age pension"" has become obsolete and inappropriate.

When the act was passed in 1927, it could be considered that reaching the age of 70 marked a giant stride on the road of life. Since that time, the legislation passed by the dominion and provincial governments for the control of contagious diseases and the promotion of public health has considerably increased the duration of human life and at 70, unlike what happened formerly, one can look forward to many years of existence, made lighter by the conveniences with which science has so wonderfully helped domestic life.

I have seen people sign their old age pension applications with some timidity, and I have also seen some persons driven to tears by the thought that such endorsement marked for them a transition which emphasized their old age. ""Old age pension"" is a hackneyed and undesirable expression. I would suggest ""family welfare allowances"", which would have a more pleasant ring and would suggest to our older citizens not the thought of impending death but the idea of serene and peaceful retirement.

Would it not be possible for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to ask the provinces for authorization to change the term ""old age pension"" to that of ""family welfare allowance""? This simple change would cast more sunshine on one of the finest social security measures put forward by this country.

1567745,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.33.14,1949-10-03,f8f904a6-1f64-4b42-94b6-dc3d21c2487c,ca.m.2011,Mr. E. A. McCusker (Regina City):,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,I should like to say a few words in this debate. I congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) on bringing this resolution before the house and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) on the saner view he takes of it. In moving his resolution I think the hon. member for Vancouver East forgot the cost entailed in implementing the services. Probably I would not speak tonight if I did not come from a province in which we have had considerable experience in socialized medicine and with these different schemes over a long number of years.

Like the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, I think that the socialists and C.C.F. are too inclined to take the credit for any social services or health measures which are being implemented or extended at the present time. I would remind them that back in 1916, and earlier than that, the Liberal government of Saskatchewan introduced many health measures which were of great benefit to the people. We had then a people

who were suffering from adversity, crop failures and one thing and another. We had a portion of our people who were unable to meet their obligations and receive the attention that they required. A number of schemes were put into operation. In one of those a municipal doctor was introduced and the municipality gave a basic guarantee of salary to the doctor to enable him to come in and live there while he provided medical services for the community. Municipal hospitals were put into effect. Contributions were made by people at large. Those within the municipality itself who were unable to pay their municipal bill were assisted by those who were in more fortunate circumstances. Municipal health schemes were introduced many years ago by Dr. Seymour, who was then the deputy minister of health in Saskatchewan. The Saskatchewan tuberculosis league was an outstanding example of what a community can do in the treatment of disease. This organization was made up of officers from the rural municipality and officers from the urban communities, citizens at large and members of the government. They set up the committee which handled the tuberculosis hospitals of Saskatchewan. I believe it was then that free hospitalization first came into effect and not in recent years, as our friends from the C.C.F. party would have us believe. However, this was done under the control of a sane nonpolitical body, which sought no kudos for what they were doing. Expenses were controlled and I need not say anything about the work that they have carried on. All hon. members know that in Saskatchewan today we have the lowest incidence of tuberculosis to be found anywhere in the world, and probably the most advanced treatment. I may say that the other day in my city a tuberculosis survey was made of the population. What percentage of the population do you think was covered? Ninety-nine per cent of the people were X-rayed. That shows how conscious they are of this disease. These things have not been brought forward in recent years. It is something that has developed. You cannot give a service such as that to a people and have it accepted overnight. It must be built up gradually.

In 1930 the Saskatchewan Cancer Commission Act was introduced by Dr. Munroe. The work was developed by Dr. Uhrich, now lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan, when he was the health minister of that province. Today we have probably one of the most advanced centres for cancer treatment in the Dominion of Canada. We had there, until a few months ago when he died of a heart attack, Dr. Blair, who was director of our cancer service and who, along with Dr.
Social Security
Richards of Toronto, has contributed more to the care and treatment of cancer than anyone else in this country. It was sane treatment gradually developed.

During my election campaign I expressed myself openly and wholeheartedly in favour of a contributory old age pension without a means test. I believe in the contributory feature of it. In the constituency I have the honour to represent there are a large number of people who have been ordinary labourers. They have worked on the streets -worked here, and worked there. The more frugal among them during the years have been able to purchase their modest homes, develop good gardens around them, and grow some of their winter supplies. However, they have not been able to put aside quite enough to look after their security in old age.

In order to be eligible for old age pension they would have to pass means tests. Some worthless galoot down the street, who had never done a decent day's work all his life, could get an old age pension and be just about as well off as someone else who had worked hard, been a good citizen and saved during his lifetime. Therefore I am in favour of the old age pension without a means test. But it must be a contributory pension. I do not think anything is worthwhile if one does not contribute toward it.

I am in favour of unemployment insurance, and I believe family allowances are a fine thing. I had not intended to speak long this evening, but I did wish to mention briefly the matter of health grants. Here perhaps my C.C.F. friends may give me a little assistance by handling some of my C.C.F. friends in Saskatchewan, so that I may get for the community I represent that to which it is entitled, and which it is prevented from getting today by a C.C.F. government.

As hon. members are aware, the national health program made provision for the sum of $165 million to support provincial health programs over a period of years. These grants covered public health, professional training, technical training, public health research-and it goes on down the line until it comes to hospital construction.

The Regina General hospital built a wing at a cost of $800,000. Construction had been started before the health grant became effective. I believe that date was April of 1948. At any rate, the hospital was partly constructed by that time, so that the city was not entitled to the total amount of the grant. The hospital authorities felt that $225,000 was coming to them from the federal government by way of grant, and an equal sum of $225,000 was coming from the provincial government. It will be recalled that
Social Security
federal health grants were to be matched by the provincial governments, in hospital construction.

When the campaign started last spring the city of Regina had received no grant. The hospital wing was completed, but remained empty because they had not sufficient money to purchase furniture. I made a public statement at that time, and the result was that there was an agreement to match $75,000 of the grant so that the hospital could buy furniture and open the wing. There was a waiting list of 300 people to get into the hospital. The building was there, but the provincial government refused to match the grant so that furniture could be purchased. The hospital had expended its funds. When I hear these great humanitarians talking I want to let them know just what the truth is, and just how human they are. They have matched $75,000 of that grant, but there is still over $100,000 which has not been received.
column2: The dominion government has

column1: agreed that the city is entitled to $175,000. Thus far the provincial government has matched only $75,000 of this amount. The taxpayers of Regina are forced to find out of taxes another $200,000, to which they are rightfully entitled by way of hospital grants.

So that if my hon. friends to my left who get their inspiration from there, and who seem to send inspiration out to them, can induce them to match this grant, I am sure my constituents in Regina city would be most grateful.
I believe I have said all I wish to say at this time.

Cruickshank (Fraser Valley):,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief. First I should like to congratulate the hon. member who preceded me. I believe his profession permits him to have a thorough knowledge about the subject concerning which he spoke. May I also say a good word for my friend from Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I did not hear all he said, but, with the exception of one or two particulars, I approve of the resolution.

In particular I should like to associate myself with what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), that no party or individual has any monopoly on the desire to foster legislation of this kind. I agree entirely with the hon. member when he says that no member or party should attempt to claim that he or they alone desire to foster social security.

Like the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker), I committed myself during the election, before the election, and after the election. I believe in a compulsory contributory insurance scheme for all people,
without a means test-and I believe that everyone in my riding is of the same opinion.

We have heard a good deal about dominion-provincial relations. Only two provinces balked at it before, and if they do not want to come in, then I believe the other eight provinces should not be deprived of the right to compulsory contributory protection by way of health insurance, or whatever one may wish to call it. I do not like the term ""old age pensions"", and I think some other name might be substituted.

I intend to support the resolution. It does not go as far as I should like to have it go, but I believe in a general way it embraces things which people in my constituency want. While I am not mentioning the names of the two provinces to which I referred, yet I feel that if they do not wish to come in, certainly the other eight provinces should not be penalized. I commend the hon. member upon his resolution. I do not happen to have a mother-in-law, but I like to tell stories. However, I do not like jokes on mothers-in-law. A person is very fortunate to have one.

If I may speak on behalf of the people in my constituency, I would say we are entirely in favour of what the resolution suggests. We think the government should not delay in bringing legislation down. Eight provinces have expressed a desire, while only two remain outside.

Eyre (Timmins):,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to hon. members who have spoken thus far concerning this resolution. May I take this opportunity to place myself on record as being in favour of the government's formulating a program of insurance which would be national in scope and sufficient to cover all citizens regardless of their age, or at any age, who, through permanent sickness or injury, become unemployable.

In my opinion this should be on a contributory basis, within the framework of our present system of unemployment insurance. May I at this time be permitted to bring to the attention of the house notices of motions Nos. 7, 12 and 23. Those three resolutions cover most of the reforms which I should like to see put into force.

During the past few months as mayor of Timmins I have witnessed a mine dispensing with the services of a considerable number of its old employees because of sickness, or for other reasons. The majority of these men had been employed by this particular mine for over 25 years and most of them have no income apart from a limited unemployment insurance benefit which will give them a small monthly income for about a year. In every case they are not eligible for old age
pensions. In a year or two these men who have been discharged will have to seek financial aid from the municipality or some other source.

I am quite aware that because of the uncertain life of a gold mine there are many factors that would have to be ironed out before a retirement plan could be instituted, and the majority of the gold mines in my constituency have had no retirement plans to date. To the best of my knowledge there is only one which has a plan formulated on paper. No doubt this situation will correct itself in the near future, but these men will not be helped.

I think industry large and small should be compelled to institute a contributory retirement pension plan and, if not, this government should institute a plan to cover all our citizens. Timmins constituency in the Porcupine area takes in approximately 16 operating mines. We have had a very good contributory medical plan covering all mine employees and their families. I think that plan should be studied and continued along with a contributory insurance retirement pension plan.

Wright (Melfori):,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate until the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) spoke. I am sorry that in his maiden speech he should have attempted to introduce a political angle. In introducing this resolution the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) tried to keep the debate on such a plane that all hon. members could express their opinions without introducing a political angle. As a member from Saskatchewan, I do not think anyone can say that I have tried to derive political advantage from the things which may have been done in that province.

It is true that in Saskatchewan we have not been able to take as great advantage of the dominion government's dollar for dollar offer as we would have been had our government not been carrying on an aggressive hospitalization scheme for some two or three years prior to the dominion scheme being introduced. The fact is that we have the largest number of hospital beds per thousand of population of any province in the dominion.

That province, as well as the provinces of Manitoba and Alberta, has become very health conscious, not just in recent years but over a long period of time. It is true, as the hon. member for Regina City said, that there have been municipal hospital and medical care schemes for a number of years. It is true also that we have had tuberculosis clinics and free hospitalization for tubercular
Social Security
patients for some twenty years. This is made possible by taxes levied by the municipalities and through grants from the provincial government.

The hon. member left the wrong impression as far as cancer treatment is concerned. The hon. member stated that cancer treatment had been started long before the present government started in Saskatchewan, but the fact is that free cancer treatment came into effect after the C.C.F. government was elected and introduced the scheme.

I do not want to become too political in connection with this thing, and I am going to leave it at that. I ask any hon. member who is interested in what has been accomplished there to get the facts and consider them for himself.

There are two points in connection with this resolution which appeal to me. One is the fact that it is asking for an integrated scheme for the whole of Canada, a minimum standard of social security for everyone in the dominion, instead of a hodgepodge scheme built up by introducing certain social security measures which are under provincial jurisdiction in some places and under dominion jurisdiction in others. In the case of children's allowances, I understand in seven provinces the administration is provincial whereas in two provinces these allowances are administered by the dominion government. Such a mix-up in administration makes it more costly.

It is only by having an integrated scheme arrived at by the provinces and the dominion getting together that we can hope to have social security at a reasonable cost and where everyone will contribute and feel that any benefit derived is a right.

Then with respect to the contributory feature, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has stated, the only way that social security can be paid for is by the work and labour of the people who produce the goods and services. I have heard the hon. members say that we in the C.C.F. expect these things to come from heaven or somewhere else, that their cost is going to come out of the large corporations or the men who have a million dollars; but social security can come from no one but the people who produce the goods and services, the men who sweat to raise food and the men who work in the factories to produce our goods and services. That is the only way that we can provide our older and indigent people with what they need.
There is no argument about our ability to produce. Every year we produce to an extent

Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):,Minister of National Health and Welfare,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,I think it may be desirable for me to take part in the debate at this stage and give an indication to the house generally of how the government views this particular resolution. May I say in the first place that I join with hon. members in expressing the conviction that an objective discussion of this matter is in the interests not only of good debate but also of a fuller appreciation of all the complexities involved in a resolution of this character.

I should also like to say that today we hear a good deal of indirect and suggestive criticism of what is called in many quarters the ""welfare state"". I want to say right here and now that I am not quite sure what precisely is meant by those who use the phrase ""welfare state"", but I suspect that their criticisms of the welfare programs of this and other countries carry with them the intention of trying to criticize social security programs generally. If by the ""welfare state"" is meant a government of a country providing for its aged; providing for those who, because of want of economic resources, are denied the best of hospital and medical care; providing children with the opportunity of attending school until the statutory school age limit and providing them with as great an amount of nutrition and general opportunity as possible, if by the ""welfare state"" is meant that the state must have a continuing interest in the welfare of those groups in the nation who must look to the state for assistance in one way or another, then I am afraid that those who use that term for critical purposes will find that most people in Canada believe in that type of welfare state.

The other day the same observation was made by the President of the United States. Therefore I suggest to those who use this phrase disapprovingly that they take serious account of the implications that are involved in their criticisms. If by ""welfare state"" they mean that we shall set up a system of statism or of socialism in its broad sense, then of course their criticism may have greater merit; but to suggest that the welfare state, in the sense in which it has been developed in most countries of the world, is in itself a sinister
thing is to say something with which I would want to take serious issue at the outset of my remarks.

The resolution of the hon. member will bear repetition. While it does contain in its generality something that most of us can accept, certainly, speaking as a member of the government, I must give it the most careful analysis, and suggest that it may contain implications that were not in the mind of the hon. member who proposed the resolution. The resolution reads:

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should seek the co-operation of the provinces for the purpose of formulating a program of social security that will be national in scope, adequate in its provisions, and that will cover all citizens of Canada in every circumstance where the individual or the family is, for any reason, deprived of the opportunity of earning a living.

On the question of co-operation with the provinces, may I say that not only should this government co-operate with the provinces towards the attainment of the objectives envisaged in the resolution, but this government continues almost daily that very type of co-operation. The co-operation formally began in 1945 when, at a conference in another part of this building, the provinces and the dominion sat down to discuss certain proposals which the dominion government offered to the then nine provinces of Canada. A subsequent conference was held a year later. Those two conferences followed one held in this chamber in January, 1941. Since that time, in spite of the failure to arrive at an understanding or agreement in full conference, there have been bilateral discussions and agreements on tax matters between the dominion government on the one hand and seven provincial governments on the other.

Since that time there have been, as I said a moment ago, continuing discussions with the provinces. Only this morning I had a discussion with a representative of a provincial government with respect to a matter that would be involved in this resolution. I offer the suggestion that our experience in the holding of open conferences perhaps will suggest to our minds that the most effective way by which to achieve the desired objectives is not necessarily to proceed at once with a full conference, but to carry on talks as they are now being carried on in certain fields for purposes of exploration with the provinces. Of course sooner or later, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has already indicated in the letter he has written to all of the provincial premiers, it will be necessary to have a larger conference as a result of the preparatory work that may have taken place.
Therefore I can agree at once with that part of the resolution which says:
. . . the government should seek the co-operation of the provinces for the purpose of formulating a program of social security that will be national in scope, adequate in its provisions . . .

I think I should at once enter a caveat that what will be ""adequate"" will be a subject of controversy. As Mr. Marsh says in his report of 1943, I believe it is, what is adequate in terms of social security benefits is a matter that involves a variety of opinions, and I would not be honest with the house if I said anything other than what I have already stated in this chamber, that social security benefits by their very nature are by way of maintenance grants.

As to suggesting a particular figure for old age pensions, for instance, I have never heard a figure suggested that could in the truest sense of the word be said to be an adequate old age pension. Even the highest figure given in this house, or now in existence in any country, might be interpreted, and I think possibly with justification by most, as not being wholly adequate in the fullest sense of the word. What we can hope to do is to try to obtain a system of social security benefits that will be as generous as it is possible to have under all the circumstances.

On a resolution like this, as the minister charged with the responsibility for many of these matters, in my analysis this evening I think the house would expect me not merely to dismiss some phases of this resolution but to show why there are difficulties in accepting it in full measure as it is presented to us. To do so, I think I should show what we have done, the cost involved in what we have done, and what we hope will be other projects to be carried out, indicating in this way the possibility of expansion; for nothing would be more dangerous than to embark suddenly upon a particular social security measure without a full appreciation of all the economic factors involved. To do that would be to prejudice the possibility of ever having a complete social security program. When I brought in the first amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act in my name as minister, and it was suggested that the amount was not large enough, I think hon. members will remember that I agreed. I said it was not as large as the government would like to see it or as I was sure the house generally would like to see it, but that in fixing that particular amount the government had exercised its judgment having in mind other social security measures. So I am sure that when I indicate to the house the cost involved, not only in what we are now doing but in what may perhaps
Social Security
be done in future, I am sure there will be general acceptance of the word of caution I am now expressing.

I have dealt with the fact that we are co-operating. I have indicated that we have certain proposals whose objectives still represent the policy of this government, and that we are proceeding in the light of our experience in what we consider the most effective way to attain those objectives. But I would not want anyone to think from reading this resolution that no substantial steps have been taken already in the development of a social security program in this country. As an authority from the university of Columbia said about two years ago, speaking at Lake Couchiching, Canada's social security program as of that date- and it has expanded very considerably since that time-was a rounded, responsible scheme of social security that would commend itself to any reasonable student in any part of the world. When you examine the monetary returns from family allowances, old age pensions, unemployment insurance benefits and the various financial opportunities given under the veterans' legislation, it will be found that in terms of dollars and cents our record will stand against that of any country in the world with the exception of four individual states in the republic to the south. That is a fact of great note which must be borne in mind in considering whether or not we have, for the time being, a program that can commend itself to reasonable men and women throughout the country who believe in a responsibly-conceived program of social security.

One of the more recent steps, of course, was the national health program announced by the then Prime Minister a little more than a year and a half ago. It should not be forgotten also that in 1947 and 1949 important amendments were made to the Old Age Pensions Act, not only with respect to the aged but also with regard to our blind citizens; and those amendments had the effect of increasing the number of old age pensioners in Canada from some 225,000 to the present figure of something like 280,000, out of the 550,000 aged citizens of this country. At the same time, provision was made through an amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act to lower the age of qualification by blind pensioners from forty to twenty-one years.

Those were measures of great substance. In 1946 we spent on old age pensions, on federal account, some $42,800,000. Today, following those amendments, we are spending $90,000,000 on old age pensions. That is only our share. When it is remembered that in addition to their supplementary payments
Social Security
the provinces pay 25 per cent of the basic pension, it will be appreciated that this represents a very substantial series of amendments.

It will be recalled that last year the basic old age pension was increased from $30 to $40. That placed us at the highest level for old age pension returns of any country in the world. At the same time we effected amendments to the Family Allowances Act eliminating the decreasing scale after the fourth child, which represented an additional financial obligation of between six and eight million dollars in the current year. We also provided that the qualifying period of three years should be reduced to one year. That was a substantial series of amendments, which one would want to consider in discussing this resolution. And concurrently with those measures, in addition to the initial steps that had been taken, increased provision was made for veterans through various amendments to the pension and war veterans' allowance legislation. This liberalization of pensions and allowances has supplemented the outstanding treatment and rehabilitation program which was developed by the Department of Veterans Affairs under the leadership of the late Senator Mackenzie, and which is now being carried on by my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg).

Those are recent amendments, Mr. Speaker. I have not dealt with the body of the existing program of social security; but I suggest that one must deal with the body of our program to appreciate this resolution in its perspective and its full purport. In the last two decades we have adopted advanced and mature lines of social progress. When I tell the house that in the coming fiscal year Canada will have allotted more than $800 million for social security measures, on federal account alone, I am sure I am making a statement which in itself will confirm all that I have said thus far to the effect that we have developed our social security program in a very thorough manner. When you consider what other countries are spending on social security and compare it with what Canada is spending, I am sure on serious reflection no one will doubt that we have indeed a program of the greatest proportions, of which we have every reason to be proud.

Tonight we have had some discussion about old age pensions. The introduction of our Old Age Pensions Act in 1927 has resulted in the federal government alone since that time spending $625 million. At the present time some 280,000 Canadians are receiving pension assistance. As a result of the amendments to which I have already referred, as I said a moment ago, we shall this year be spending on current account $90 million alone on old age pensions, not includ-
ing what the provinces are paying in respect of their 25 per cent or by way of supplementary payments.

As was stated by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the goal of the government is toward a system of contributory old age pensions. But as one who in these past two and a half years has had to give a good deal of thought to this matter, let me say clearly that I have used the word ""goal"" because I want to be fully honest with the house. We have not now in this parliament the power to enact a compulsory system of old age pensions on a contributory basis. As forecast in the speech from the throne, we are taking steps to acquire the power to amend the constitution of this country by our own agency. When that power has been acquired, discussion will inevitably arise with the provinces as to their attitude with regard to endowing the federal government with the necessary power to enact such a measure if, after the most careful analysis, it is thought that is the best course for Canada and for her aged citizens, and is the most effective way of bringing about what we all hope will even yet be a more perfect system for old age retirement.

Let me at once explain why I speak in this way. Recently in the United States we have seen agreements between management and labour with regard to pension schemes where the element of contribution has been completely removed. What will be the effect of those agreements upon schemes which the state may want to sponsor remains to be seen. Only last week I took advantage of my presence at the United Nations meetings to discuss with the representatives of two countries, including the United States, then-experience with regard to a great number of industrial pension schemes existing in those countries. It is amazing to find the number of noncontributory schemes that are in existence. It is much greater, I am sure, than the house at the moment perhaps realizes. What the tendency will be is a matter that we must look at clearly. It may be that a great section of our public, when it ascertains that there are to be these noncontributory schemes, may feel that a noncontributory scheme is the best thing for Canada. At the moment that is not my view. At the moment I believe in a contributory system, one that will put into the hands of the recipients the opportunity of building up a fund for his or her retirement period. But as I say, having made that assertion I must qualify it by pointing out the difficulties, such as the constitutional position for one thing, and, for another, the development of new schemes on a broad scale, much broader than perhaps many anticipated a few years ago. But in

spite of all this, my thinking at the moment suggests that, just as with unemployment insurance, so too with old age pensions, we may possibly be approaching the period when we can give active consideration to a scheme on a contributory basis.

But I want the house to appreciate fully that the position I am now taking is one by way of objective, as a goal, rather than a positive statement; because that can only be given after the fullest discussion with the provinces and with others concerned.

,Liberal,,Paul Joseph James Martin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Joseph William Noseworthy,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=44449e3c-562a-4461-aa3d-ae59eb3971cd&Language=E&Section=ALL
1567753,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.33.22,1949-10-03,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin:,Minister of National Health and Welfare,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,The hon. member wishes to introduce a political note, but I think the house will appreciate that I am trying to deal with this matter in a responsible manner in keeping with the way in which the resolution itself was introduced in this house.

Then there is the matter of unemployment insurance by which 3,350,000 workers now are provided with a reserve of well over half a billion dollars; the veterans' charter; the legislation providing for support for farm and fish prices. All these are important steps in providing social security for those in the nation who require it. In our family allowances measure we have perhaps the most effective single act of social security ever introduced by any country in any part of the world. We were not the first to introduce family allowances, but our level of family allowances is higher than that of any other country. Our system was the first to take on the character of full government participation without contribution from parents or guardians or from industry. We have the benefit of the experience of family allowance schemes in France, Belgium and Switzerland, where such schemes have been in existence for many years. Because we were so desirous of avoiding the use of family allowances as a means of depressing wages, we removed the contribution from industry in order that there could be no excuse or deliberate effort made to use family allowances as an occasion to depress wages.

In considering, as the resolution suggests, that we should formulate a program of social security that will be national in scope, surely this measure of family allowances has a great role to play. Last June-on June 1, to be exact-we made a payment to an individual parent representing the attainment of one billion dollars in family allowance payments since the period of inauguration of that particular measure. When it is remembered that family allowance cheques go out each month now to at least 4,100,000 children, representing 1,800,000 families, spending this year alone for that purpose the sum of $290 million, it
Social Security

will be appreciated that we in this country have embarked on a substantial social security program. Leaving out family allowances and the veterans' charter, and taking particularly unemployment insurance-the power for which came to us as a result of a constitutional amendment consented to by the provinces-and old age pensions, in those two measures we, within the provinces, have enjoyed, on the whole, a great measure of co-operation. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) say tonight that he was not advocating a system of centralized control or administration. Surely anyone who has given this subject much thought will agree at once with that proposition. For any federal state like Canada to try to centralize administration or even to assume full financial responsibility is not realistic and, I submit, not desirable. The moment we take away from the provinces or, in some instances, from the municipality, some responsibility in the matter of social welfare, to that extent I think we shall seriously prejudice the development of a system of social security in Canada. That is why, in so far as we can in health, in old age pensions, and in most of these other measures now in existence or developing, we must seek to have schemes that involve provincial as well as federal interest and federal action.

Another measure that I want to mention tonight as part of this program that we have now and that is developing is our national health program. This is by no means an insignificant measure. It is a measure which, when it was introduced, received, as one would expect, the full approbation of this house, as indeed it received it from all of the provincial governments in Canada but one who expressed themselves on it. That measure is an important one. It represents, as the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) said earlier tonight, the determination of this government, or of this parliament, to expend within a period of five years from the date of the announcement of the program $165 million for the purpose of helping the provinces, where resides the primary constitutional responsibility for matters of health, to enable such provincial governments to accelerate their public health programs through campaigns for tuberculosis control; for crippling conditions in children; campaigns in connection with venereal disease; campaigns to encourage scientific research along medical lines; to encourage professional training; to encourage cancer control; to give impetus to hospital construction programs in this country. All of that is part of a program which serves as a pre-
Social Security
requisite tor a soundly constructed scheme along responsible lines for medical and hospital care.

If for any reason one wants to depreciate that program, let me refer right now to the words used by the American public health association a year ago when commenting upon Canada's national health program in the United States. I should make this observation. They have developed a system of health grants just like our own. Our grants on a per capita basis are greater than every grant which the federal government in that country provides for the purpose of assisting the state governments in the discharge of their responsibilities in the formation of health policies in the United States. That surely is a matter of great significance. The very fact that in the first year it was not possible for the provinces to utilize the full amount of money made available to them indicates the generosity and the imagination of those who were responsible for this national health program. Who were responsible? The program represents the joint endeavour of both the federal and the provincial governments.

My hon. friend properly asks us to seek further ways of effecting co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. That has been done, and particularly in this instance. Before we embarked on that program we called a conference of the provinces, and the Department of National Health and Welfare met with the responsible officials from the various departments of health of the provinces. We laid before them our ideas and we obtained their reactions. In every step since then we proceeded with the provinces in a co-operative manner, trying to make the scheme more effective as the result of such co-operation. Only this morning to the extent that time allowed I took part in a conference, which is going on tomorrow morning as well, with the mental health directors of the ten provinces of Canada who are sitting down with us in our department working out schemes based upon this program and certain projects that all of us have in mind for the future. That kind of co-operation is prevailing between ourselves and the provinces. I am happy to say that such co-operation is increasing in its intensity and I think in its consequential achievements.

With regard to this plan as a prerequisite, I will simply repeat what I said on another occasion in this house. This program provides the fundamental prerequisite of a nation-wide system of health insurance. The new services being developed, and the hospitals being built with funds now provided by the federal government, are hastening the moment when in

every province it will be possible to take further action toward hospital and medical care insurance, for which of course the federal government will provide assistance under satisfactory agreements for dominion-provincial co-operation.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) shortly before the statement that I have quoted, which is mine, said:
It is up to the people and the government in each province to take the initiative in working out health insurance plans in line with their local conditions and their traditions.

That represents a carefully conceived and thought-out policy. It is based on the proposition on which this resolution itself is based, namely, that these schemes depend not on unilateral action but on co-operative action between the dominion on the one hand and the provincial governments on the other. A year and a quarter ago we had as our objective the building of forty thousand additional hospital beds in Canada. That was a project which some said was too great; it was said to be an impossible assignment or target, but because of the co-operation which we received from the provinces, and because of the financial assistance we made available to them, I am in the happy position of being able to say tonight that within the last year and a half this co-operative enterprise has resulted in the building of fourteen thousand additional hospital beds in Canada.

Now, sir, I should like to deal particularly with what I think may be considered as some weaknesses in the resolution that is now before us. With the proposition that the government should seek the co-operation of the provinces for the purpose of formulating a program of social security that would be national in scope and adequate in its provisions, I say unhesitatingly that that too is the view of the government. Not only is it our intention to continue that method of co-operation, but we have been doing that very thing. While in the last few months we may have resorted to different tactics by which to bring about certain achievements, the fact is that we subscribe fully to the terms of the resolution to the extent that I have read them. But, sir, we have a responsibility, a responsibility not only to ourselves but to the provinces and to others in the country, not to pass a resolution whose general terms are fully accepted by us, but to make sure that we have examined every implication involved in that resolution. I take second place to no one in this house in my desire to see a fully developed scheme of national security even on a more extended line than we now have in this country. But because that is my purpose I have to approach this in the

light of my responsibilities as the person and as the member of the government for the time being charged with bringing about the objectives of the resolution. The part I find some difficulty with is this:
And that will cover all citizens of Canada in every circumstance where the individual or the family is, for any reason, deprived of the opportunity of earning a living.

I do not think that, on careful analysis, we can agree exactly to that. Let me give some objections that come to my mind almost at once. First of all the words ""all citizens"" are used. We have many citizens of Canada who do not live in Canada. We have citizens who live abroad, some of them permanently abroad, whose domicile is still abroad, and who are enjoying social security benefits under other jurisdictions-or, if they are not enjoying social security benefits, are outside the reach of the government at home.

Is it intended that such individuals should be included? Let no one think for a moment that the persons who are legal citizens of Canada but whose domicile is abroad are few in number. The number is a very significant one, as my colleague the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley), I am sure, could indicate, if the question were directed to him.

Then, another objection I see to these very doubtful terms is that the resolution as a whole takes no account whatsoever of municipal responsibility. The three levels of government in this country are municipal, provincial and federal, and all three have their responsibilities. While in the first instance the responsibility of the municipality was more comprehensive than it is now, the fact is that municipalities still have their responsibilities in respect of these arrangements. Many provinces take the view that we are not encouraging sufficiently the assumption of responsibility by the municipalities in their particular areas.

But they have to be taken into consideration. There are many cases of hardship that can even at this time be best taken care of by municipalities. They are not cases of a type; they are individual special cases. In Great Britain, in New Zealand, in Australia, that local responsibility has not been taken away. In those countries, likewise, every citizen is not covered, in the sense that this resolution envisages, by the social security provisions to be found in those countries.

Then again-and I have to interpret the resolution very strictly, because of its implications-this resolution in its final terms does not take into consideration a citizen or individual who might himself be guilty of an act which would put him out of the wage-earning market, or the income-earning market; and 45781-31
Social Security

there are a few such individuals. A man could deliberately-and we have had such cases-dismember his two hands, and yet under this resolution he would be entitled to benefits. Are we going to say tonight that that kind of situation should be condoned by a legislative body?

,Liberal,,Paul Joseph James Martin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83&Language=E&Section=ALL

1567755,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.33.24,1949-10-03,7d99e6fa-2ea6-461d-a602-f3c8c754041d,ca.m.8259,Mr. Marlin:,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,My hon. friends laugh. But we are legislators. We are called upon tonight to pass a resolution; and our responsibility and our duty is to make sure that that legislation covers every case which at the moment of deliberation we are able to think of. It is my responsibility as Minister of National Health and Welfare to indicate what I believe to be some of the inadequacies and weaknesses in the resolution as at present drawn.

Another more serious objection is that the mover of the resolution uses the words ""that will cover all citizens of Canada."" But we have not made citizenship a condition for obtaining social security benefits. A child does not have to be a citizen under the Family Allowances Act in order to be eligible for the family allowance. An old age pensioner does not have to be a citizen of Canada to get an old age pension. A man does not have to be a citizen of Canada to be a beneficiary under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Yet this resolution would go farther, and would restrict not only future legislation but existing legislation.

It calls upon us to pass legislation, with the active co-operation of the provinces, provided it is given to all citizens of Canada. Let me repeat that we give social security benefits in this country in respect of the various acts I have mentioned, not on the basis of nationality, not on the basis of citizenship, but on the mere fact of residence; and this resolution does not take that into consideration.

The final observation I would make in this particular is to indicate, as I said at the outset, that there is no country in the world with a provision of this kind. Take a country where, it may be suggested, social security benefits are most comprehensive-and it has been suggested the United Kingdom is such a country; for the purposes of argument let us accept that suggestion. But in the United Kingdom there is no social security measure which provides social security assistance for all citizens of the United Kingdom in every circumstance where an individual or family is for any reason deprived of the opportunity of earning a living.
I say that to have a resolution couched in those terms-I was going to say ""extravagant terms"", but I will not say that, because the
Social Security

hon. member who is the author of this resolution is a responsible member of the House of Commons and usually approaches discussions of these matters in a serious manner. I will not use that word; but I am sure upon reflection the hon. member will find that the observations I have made are not without merit.

There is nothing further I can add except to say that, in a general way, so far as requesting the government to seek the cooperation of the provinces is concerned, we will continue to do so. That we are doing. I believe that what we are now doing will, in the course of, I trust, not too many months, be productive of good results.

Beyond that at the present time I cannot go, except to say that the government will make every effort toward expanding its program, in the light of what it believes should have priority, and in the light of what it considers to be its financial limitations- and that is something which we have to keep in mind. In the light of these things the government is not oblivious of the desirability of continuing to seek the cooperation of the provinces in expanding our social security measures.

One would not be thorough in his presentation if he did not again say that the basis of any social security system is the maintenance of peace in the world, that the productive capacity in a country should be maintained at a level whereby these things can be assured and continued.

It is true that Sir Stafford Cripps said the other day in the British House of Commons that there would be no interference with provisions for social security payments in that country. On the other hand, I can say with some authority that there are countries in continental Europe-and for fear of perhaps entering into a field in which I have no authority to make any public observations, I shall not name them-there are countries, represented by distinguished statesmen who have recently visited Canada, where very serious consideration is being given to reducing the social security payments, because of weaknesses in their productive capacity.

We do not want to be in that position; and it is because we do not want to be in that position that this government is doing all it can to make its contribution toward the preservation of peace in the world, doing all it can to extend its foreign markets so that our artisans, industrialists and farmers can sell their products, in return for which there will be guaranteed incomes to enable Canada to carry on in a responsible way these schemes of social security.

In speaking to this resolution I may say in all fairness and indisputably that the government that is now ready to seek the co-operation of the provinces has by its record to date given evidence of its determination to continue in the pursuit of that co-operation.

1567756,ca.proc.d.1949-10-03.33.25,1949-10-03,f786df30-a001-4982-becb-a5fa8e5551eb,ca.m.9516,Mr. F. D. Shaw (Red Deer):,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I are intensely interested in the resolution presently before us. Perhaps one could leave it at that and at the same time leave the impression that we are going to support it. However, having said that, perhaps I should indicate that I personally have no hesitation in indicating my readiness to support the resolution. I was rather interested in the observations of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin).

In the first place, he took considerable time to dig up-perhaps I can use that expression -every conceivable type of condition that might, either now or some time in the future, arise under this particular resolution. If every piece of legislation brought before this house by the government were considered in the same way we would be unwise to pass any of it. During the course of years that I have had the privilege of occupying a seat in this house I have heard, not one but several cabinet ministers, when questioned rather closely with respect to sections of bills, say that it would have to be left to the courts to decide. Yet in connection with this particular resolution the minister went into great detail to indicate some real and many purely imaginary conditions which could be used as an argument for casting the resolution aside.

I believe I heard the minister go so far as to say that one might cut off both his hands in order to qualify under legislation that might be brought forward as the result of passing this resolution. I am not conscious of any piece of dominion government legislation in the field of public welfare, good as much of it is, under which I would cut off even one hand in order to qualify. I am sure that most Canadians feel the same.

I agree with the minister wholeheartedly, and the resolution agrees with him, when he states that the provinces should be consulted with respect to health measures. We have always been much opposed to centralization and we feel that under centralization this type of activity could not conceivably be effective. We feel that decentralization, with administration left in the hands of the provincial governments, would bring forward much more effective results than would otherwise be the case.
We agree with the second portion of the resolution which states that any security

scheme should be national in scope. It is well known that many parts of Canada are more favourably blessed from the standpoint of resources than other parts. We realize that those areas which are so blessed could provide a higher standard of health services than many other sections. But it is Canada we are dealing with. It is the health of Canadians we are concerned with. We are most desirous of seeing that any benefits that do accrue shall accrue to the people in those areas which from an economic or national wealth point of view are not as well blessed as other parts of the country.

The minister referred specifically to the latter part of the resolution and indicated that that was why the government could not accept the resolution. I think one of the most objectionable types of cases we encounter in Canada today are those which concern persons who because of physical incapacitation are unable to earn a living. Cases come to the attention of every one of us of persons under 70 years of age who cannot qualify for benefits under the Old Age Pensions Act, who have had to leave the labour market because of physical infirmities, who have nowhere to turn to except the municipal relief offices. Personally I do not think we have succeeded in any respect in the field of social security when persons are obliged because of incapacitation to seek municipal relief.

That is one reason why we have always urged that the Old Age Pensions Act be amended or a separate act enacted to permit these persons to qualify for benefits. I would go so far as to say that the government, in co-operation with the provinces, might consider this type of legislation before extending other types of legislation which we now have on the statute books and which provide benefits to other groups of people. I would be the first to say that, as far as our Old Age Pensions Act is concerned, we have still some distance to go before the payments are sufficient to guarantee a decent living for our people; but on the other hand those people are certainly much better off under the present rate of pension than those who are physically incapacitated and not eligible for anything. I think the minister might concentrate upon the solution of that particular problem as his next objective.

I would be the last one in the world to endeavour to take any credit away from the minister or the government for what has been lone in the field of national health. I think that most of that legislation has proved beneficial to many of our Canadian people. But t recall a time when many of us were pressing for that legislation, long before it appeared 3n the statute books of our country. I can recall when many hon. gentlemen who are 45781-311
Social Security

now sitting in the house ridiculed us day in and day out for suggesting that such a thing as family allowances was possible. It is significant that since 1945, when family allowances became a reality, we have not heard that type of criticism. We pride ourselves upon the position which we took and the part which we played in persuading the government to adopt that legislation and make those allowances a reality in Canada.

As I say, we are most grateful for the legislation that has been passed to assist the Canadian people in the field of public health. We anticipate more, but we do not feel that this resolution in its present form brings forward all the evil possibilities that the minister indicated during the course of his speech. As I say, we can be assured that with the co-operation of the provinces no minister would bring in a type of legislation that would permit many of the conditions which he referred to as being dangerous under the type of legislation that he envisaged following a resolution of this character. It could be said that the resolution is nothing but objective. It could be considered as an endorsation of much that the government has already done in the field of national health and social security. It could be a directive from the house to the government to proceed further with the introduction of other measures as and when such become possible.

May I say to the minister I feel that in the absence of a certain economic policy- perhaps I can put it that way-which would remove from our society the condition under which certain people find themselves unable to procure essential health services, the government is definitely under a moral obligation to pass the necessary legislation in order to fill the gaps.

I do not desire to occupy more of the time of the house. I agree with much that has been said by previous speakers, but at the same time there is a good deal with which I do not agree. I shall not take the time at the moment, however, to point out on what grounds I disagree. I repeat that we feel there is no danger in the passage of a resolution of this kind, because we are certain that the government is not going to negotiate any agreement with the provinces under which they will clash head on with many of the difficulties which the minister enumerated.

I can think of no more intelligent way of co-operating than by co-operation through the government whereby we collectively provide for those emergencies which the individual citizen in numerous cases cannot provide for himself. Siuder (Maple Creek):,,REQUEST FOR FORMULATION OF NATIONAL PROGRAM,,,The subject matter of the resolution now before the house, Mr. Speaker, is close to the hearts of many of us, and something we can all support if the mover and seconder will word their resolution in such a way as to make it possible for all the people of Canada to receive the benefit of anything this parliament may do in regard to social welfare and security.

The resolution asks that the government seek the co-operation of the provinces to bring about these beneficial conditions. I think it is about time the provinces should seek to co-operate with the dominion government in bringing about a condition under which all the people of the country will benefit from whatever steps may be taken. Not only do I want agreement with respect to the health services of the country, about which the minister has spoken this evening; I also want agreement in regard to all the services affecting the
Social Security

people of Canada. It is impossible for a particular province to formulate a policy in regard to social services which will be permanent and of definite benefit to the people for all time. We know that from our experience in Saskatchewan; but let it be understood that the government of that province has been trying to do something, and I suggest that it be given all credit for that. It may be that it has been doing it in the wrong way, but at least the government has been trying to do something. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I believe that in the last few years the Liberal government has listened more attentively to the criticism offered by the opposition than any other government in history. Strangely enough, however, the government that listened to that criticism and benefited therefrom is here in larger numbers today than ever before, while those who delivered that criticism without stint in the past few years are here in fewer numbers than ever before. So I suggest that the criticism offered by any opposition party will be well received by the government, and I believe the opposition parties will do themselves and the people in general a service by presenting resolutions of a kind which all the people can support.

A short time ago the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) dealt with the question of social services for all Canada. Social Security

nothing in particular to do with what was offered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). Nevertheless, we could perhaps offer as an instance one little thing that happened in Saskatchewan in connection with social services. I should not like to have anyone tell anyone else about this, but they tell us out in Saskatchewan that, in connection with social services, the upkeep of the hospitalization plan is provided by contributions of the people; that is, there is a hospitalization fee in connection with the operation of that social service. They tell us that there is a law on the statute books of Saskatchewan to the effect that if anyone refuses to pay that hospitalization fee, he must either pay a fine or go to jail. I believe that is one of the things we should like to eliminate in this country of ours, in order that we would have nothing in connection with our social services that would lead one to believe that if one was not in a position to pay the required fee, or refused to pay it, a jail penalty would be imposed. We should like to have a social service that would be so comprehensive and be held in such high esteem by all the people of Canada that no one would need to attach a penalty of that kind to the law.
